text: Okay, let's dive right into the results, starting with robustness. They held the agent fixed at GPT-4o and only changed which model played the simulated user.
And that alone was enough to move the numbers?

It was. Three of the five user models, GPT-4o, Sonnet 3.7, and Kimi-K2-Thinking, land in a cluster, roughly 67 to 71 percent success rates. But swap in Sonnet 4.5 as the user, and you get almost a 9 percentage point gap versus Sonnet 3.7.
So the agent didn't change at all, just who's simulating the customer, and the score can swing by 9 points. What does that do to something like a leaderboard comparison?
It undermines it. If two teams each report a single number using a different simulated-user model, those numbers aren't really comparable, even when the underlying agent is identical.
I'd have guessed the fix is simple, just pick the strongest available model to play the user and you're covered.

You'd think so, but the data argues against it. Sonnet 3.7 is generally considered the stronger model, yet using GPT-4o as the user model produced a slightly higher success rate, 67.8 versus 67.0, and a much tighter standard deviation, 1.2 versus 3.3.
So the so-called weaker model actually gave a more stable read on the agent.
Right, which points to something other than raw capability. It looks like closeness between the agent and user model matters more than either one being the single strongest option on its own.
That's a real design implication for anyone building an eval. The user model isn't a neutral instrument, it's a variable you have to control for.
So what's actually at stake if a lab just publishes one leaderboard number without disclosing which model played the user?
Anyone downstream trusting that number to pick an agent for production. They'd be comparing apples to oranges without knowing it.

And doesn't that make it hard to trust the big jumps at face value too? They flag that it's genuinely difficult to tell whether Sonnet 4.5's jump as a user model reflects real capability gains or just that model having seen more of this kind of benchmark during training.

Fair, that contamination question is impossible to fully rule out from outside the lab. Okay, that's robustness. Now the paper pivots to validity, forget consistency across user models, are simulated users even tracking real human behavior?

Right, and they pick the friendliest possible test first. Prior work shows LLMs carry a strong Western, Anglocentric bias, so the logic is, if simulated users are going to match anyone well, it should be US participants.
So this is the best case scenario for the simulators, not a stress test.
Exactly, they're checking calibration in the setting where they'd expect the strongest alignment between simulated and human users.
And even in the best case?

Even there, agents only hit a 45.2 percent success rate with real US participants, and the calibration error between human and simulated users comes out to 15.1. That's substantial miscalibration in the most favorable setting they could construct.

Figure 2 is the picture of that, human success rate plotted against success rate with the simulated users for the US group, with that 15.1 calibration error and error bars at plus or minus one standard deviation.
And the miscalibration isn't spread evenly across task difficulty. It's worst at the first and fourth difficulty bins, where the calibration error jumps to 25.9 across just those two.
Which direction does it break in? Does the simulation make agents look better or worse than they really are?

Both, depending on where you look. On the hardest tasks it undersells the agent, human success there was 30.8 percent, and the simulated evaluation reads lower. On the moderately difficult tasks it flips and overestimates, human success there was 39.0 percent.
So an agent could look artificially weak on the hard tasks and artificially strong on the medium ones, in the same benchmark, at the same time.
If it's this skewed even in the friendliest test case, what does that mean for people actually deciding which agent to ship based on these scores?

It means the number on the leaderboard could be quietly wrong in either direction, and you wouldn't know which. And apparently this is just the calibration story averaged across everyone. Next part digs into who this fails hardest for, the fairness findings are coming, and from the sound of it, that's where it gets uncomfortable.
